s: B. The Takings Clause.
"Nor shall private property be taken for public use, without just compensation."
The clause was the first provision of the Bill of Rights incorporated, in Chicago, Burlington & Quincy R.R. v. Chicago (1897).
It does not bar takings; it conditions them.
Public use.
The phrase is read broadly as "public purpose."
Berman v. Parker (1954) upheld urban renewal, and Hawaii Housing Authority v. Midkiff (1984) upheld land redistribution.
Kelo v. City of New London (2005) upheld a taking for private economic development under a comprehensive plan.
The decision provoked widespread state-law reforms.
Just compensation is fair market value at the time of the taking.
A property owner may sue in federal court as soon as the government takes property without paying (Knick v. Township of Scott, 2019, overruling Williamson County).
A county that keeps surplus proceeds from a tax-foreclosure sale beyond the debt owed effects a taking (Tyler v. Hennepin County, 2023).
Takings analysis.
Physical appropriation or occupation is a per se taking regardless of size: Loretto (1982, cable box), Cedar Point Nursery v. Hassid (2021, union access regulation), Horne (2015, raisin reserve).
Total wipeout.

Regulation denying all economically beneficial use is a per se taking unless background principles of nuisance and property law already prohibited the use (Lucas v. South Carolina Coastal Council, 1992).
Everything else: Penn Central balancing (1978):
the economic impact on the claimant;
interference with distinct, investment-backed expectations;
the character of the government action (physical invasion versus adjusting benefits and burdens).
The parcel is defined as a whole, using a multi-factor test for the relevant unit (Murr v. Wisconsin, 2017).
Exactions.
Permit conditions must have an essential nexus to a legitimate state interest (Nollan, 1987) and rough proportionality to the project's impact (Dolan, 1994).
This applies to monetary exactions (Koontz, 2013) and to legislatively imposed conditions (Sheetz v. County of El Dorado, 2024).
"Substantially advances" is not a takings test (Lingle v. Chevron, 2005).
